analysis.one_liner: Sets a national goal to cut U.S. oil use and subsidizes electric vehicles, biofuels, and natural gas.
analysis.headline: Introduced nine days before the session ended, the bill was sent to seven committees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a national goal of cutting U.S. oil consumption by 8 million barrels a day by 2030, coordinated from the White House. It would tighten fuel economy and emissions standards for cars and nonroad vehicles, spend heavily to speed up electric vehicle adoption — including up to $250 million grants to selected communities, bigger and refundable tax credits for EV buyers, and charging-station loan guarantees — and extend tax credits for biofuels and natural gas vehicles. It died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, through stricter fuel economy standards for model years 2017-2030 that would lower gasoline bills; EV buyers in selected deployment communities, who would get a refundable credit raised from $2,500 to $5,000 that could be applied at the dealership; commuters, through a higher tax-exempt transit benefit; workers trained for EV maintenance and charging installation jobs; and state and local governments chosen as deployment communities. Electric vehicle and battery makers, electric utilities, biofuel producers, and the natural gas industry would receive large new subsidies and mandates that channel customers and federal money to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, EV buyers, and clean-energy industries

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national goal of reducing U.S. oil consumption by 8 million barrels per day by 2030 and directs the President to write and update a national oil independence plan.

Requires joint fuel efficiency and greenhouse gas standards for cars for model years 2017-2030 and for nonroad vehicles like rail, marine, and construction engines, which would lower fuel costs for vehicle owners.

Authorizes $2 billion for a targeted electric vehicle deployment communities program, with grants of up to $250 million per community, and requires each deployment community to give residents who buy an EV at least $2,500 in local consumer benefits on top of federal incentives.

Makes the EV tax credit refundable for buyers in deployment communities, raises it to $5,000, lets buyers transfer it to the dealer or lender at purchase, and raises the per-manufacturer cap from 200,000 to 300,000 vehicles.
Authorizes $150 million for workforce training programs for first responders, electricians, engineers, inspectors, and mechanics working on electric vehicles and charging infrastructure.
Raises the tax-exempt commuter transit benefit to $230 per month, which reduces the after-tax cost of commuting by transit or vanpool.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through billions in authorized spending ($2 billion for deployment communities, $150 million for training, a $1 billion tax-exempt bond program, loan guarantees for charging infrastructure) and through the lost revenue from extended and expanded tax credits for biofuels, natural gas vehicles, and EV charging equipment. Electric utility ratepayers could bear grid-upgrade costs, though regulators could allow utilities to recover them. Oil producers and refiners would lose sales as the standards and electrification programs shrink petroleum demand.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, ratepayers, and the oil industry

drawbacks.text: The bill would spend billions and hand out many new tax expenditures, including a $1 billion tax-credit bond program and grants of up to $250 million per community, at a time when the cost of each program would fall on federal taxpayers.

It would pick technology winners by directing concentrated federal support to plug-in electric vehicles, batteries, natural gas vehicles, and biofuels rather than setting neutral goals; it even reclassifies algae-based fuel as cellulosic biofuel to qualify it for existing credits.

It would create a new White House National Energy Security Council and multiple advisory committees, task forces, studies, and model-code programs, adding administrative machinery whose value depends entirely on execution.
It would require every electric utility to develop and periodically update an EV-support plan, with administrative costs that utilities could seek to recover from ratepayers.
The oil-consumption goal includes an escape hatch: the President could adjust the 8-million-barrel target after weighing economic costs, so the headline number was not guaranteed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-interest case is real: tighter fuel standards save drivers money at the pump, and cutting oil dependence reduces exposure to volatile world oil prices. But the bill pursues that goal mainly by routing large subsidies through specific industries — EV and battery makers, utilities, biofuel and natural gas producers — with limited cost controls and several new bureaucratic layers, and it includes a built-in waiver for the headline oil-savings target. A leaner version could have pursued the same ends at much lower cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 21, 2010, nine days before the Congress ended, referred to seven House committees, and none of them ever held a hearing or voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Inslee introduced the bill with Rep. Michael Castle as its only cosponsor, on December 21, 2010.

The House referred it to seven committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Budget, Science and Technology, Oversight and Government Reform, and Natural Resources — with consideration 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker.'
No committee took any further action: the record shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, petroleum producers and refiners faced no new fuel economy escalation, no 8-million-barrel reduction program, and no new environmental rules on federal-land drilling, while taxpayers never took on the bill's multi-billion-dollar subsidy commitments. Electric vehicle and battery makers received none of the deployment grants and credits they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers; taxpayers spared new subsidies

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but with no votes ever taken there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would set a goal of cutting U.S. oil use by 8 million barrels a day, tighten fuel economy standards through 2030, and impose environmental best-practice rules on oil and gas operators on federal lands, all of which would shrink petroleum demand and revenue.

The bill would channel billions through these firms: a $2 billion deployment communities program, a raised and refundable EV buyer credit (up to $5,000) with a higher per-maker cap, loan guarantees for charging networks, and a federal battery prize and R&D funding. Drivers would get cleaner, cheaper-to-run cars, but the policy would permanently route the public's electrification push through these companies' products.

Every utility would have to write and update an EV-support plan, and regulators could allow cost recovery from ratepayers; utilities would also be eligible issuers of the new $1 billion tax-credit bonds for charging infrastructure. EV adoption grows their electricity sales, with grid costs partly borne by all customers.

The bill would create an investment tax credit for advanced biofuel facilities, add algae to the cellulosic biofuel definition, and extend biodiesel, renewable diesel, and alcohol fuel credits. Alternative fuels displace oil, but the credits come at taxpayer cost.

New tax credits for natural gas vehicles, tax-exempt natural gas vehicle bonds, and an expensing deduction for plants making compressed or liquefied natural gas vehicles. Natural gas displaces petroleum but is still a fossil fuel.

Buyers could transfer their refundable EV credit to the selling dealer or the financing company at the point of sale, with a window-sticker disclosure and a requirement that the transferee pass the full credit through as a price reduction.
